scenario: AITA for not being emotional on my wedding day? | My wife and I didn’t do many traditional things for our wedding. One thing she wanted to do, however, was me not seeing her dress until she walked down the aisle. I agreed. She kept saying I’d love it, she loved it. She and her best friend (maid of honor) kept sharing reaction posts of grooms happy crying upon getting a first look at their bride, tagging me in it, saying “this will be you!” Day of, wife walks down. She herself did look beautiful, as always. However, I was not big on the dress. To me, it wasn’t at all flattering. But I didn’t focus on that. I focused on her. I smiled. I didn’t break down in tears like some reaction pics/videos. The maid of honor kept nudging me until I looked at her and mouthed “stop”. We got married, kissed, the whole thing. Everything was fine at the reception. Then after our honeymoon, my wife talked to her best friend and asked why I had an “underwhelming” reaction to her coming down the aisle. I said I didn’t. She said there are pictures that guests took and I don’t look how she pictured. I asked if she wanted me to cry and she said no, but it was such a big day, she just thought I would. I said I was estatic to marry her and that showed, without me being over dramatic. I also said I had her friend nudging me the whole time and that was unfair to me. Finally I asked if we had a wedding or a play, because I never got lines. Now she’s mad at me. Am I an ass here? I do feel bad she’s disappointed but I couldn’t force myself to have a reaction.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me to not be emotional on my wedding day, especially regarding my wife's dress. Let me start by understanding the situation better. My wife and I didn't do many traditional things for our wedding, which is fine with me. One thing she really wanted was for me not to see her dress until she walked down the aisle. I agreed to that, thinking it would be a nice surprise. She kept telling me she knew I'd love it, and she loved it too. She and her best friend, who was the maid of honor, kept showing me pictures of grooms crying when they first see their brides, tagging me in and saying, "This will be you!" So, I guess she expected me to have a strong emotional reaction when I saw her. On the day of the wedding, my wife walked down the aisle, and she looked beautiful, as always. But honestly, I wasn't that impressed with the dress. To me, it didn't look flattering. But I didn't focus on that; I focused on her. I smiled, and I didn't break down into tears like some of the reaction pictures and videos I saw. The maid of honor kept nudging me, trying to get me to look at the dress, and even mouthed "stop" to me. We got married, kissed, and everything went fine at the reception. After our honeymoon, my wife talked to her best friend about why I had such an underwhelming reaction to her walking down the aisle. She said there were pictures that guests took, and I didn't look how she pictured. She asked if I wanted to cry, and I said no, but it was such a big day, she just thought I would. I told her I was ecstatic to marry her, and that showed without me being overly dramatic. I also mentioned that the maid of honor was nudging me the whole time, which was unfair to me. Finally, I asked if we had a wedding or a play because I never got any lines. Now she's mad at me. I do feel bad that she's disappointed, but I couldn't force myself to have a reaction. So, is it right or wrong for me to not be emotional on my wedding day? Let me think about this. First, I need to consider what emotions are appropriate for a wedding day. Weddings are supposed to be joyful and emotional events, celebrating the union of two people. It's common for people to cry or get overwhelmed with emotions on such a significant day. However, everyone experiences emotions differently. Some people are more reserved, while others are more expressive. It's possible that I'm just not the type to cry or get overly emotional in public, even on such a special day. Another point to consider is the expectation set by my wife and her best friend. They showed me pictures of grooms crying, implying that this was the expected reaction. But if I'm not the type to cry, does that make me wrong? Or is it just a difference in how we express emotions? Also, the fact that the maid of honor was nudging me and trying to get me to look at the dress might have added to the pressure. It's unfair to feel like I have to perform a certain way just because it's expected. Moreover, I focused on my wife and the significance of the day rather than the dress. That seems like a positive thing, valuing the person over the material aspects of the wedding. But my wife is disappointed because she felt that my reaction didn't match her expectations. She might feel that I didn't fully appreciate the effort she put into the day, especially the dress. So, is it right or wrong? It seems like it's more about differing expectations and how emotions are expressed. It's not necessarily right or wrong, but it's a matter of communication and understanding each other's perspectives. I should probably talk to my wife about how I felt and why I didn't express emotions in the way she expected. It's important to address her feelings and explain my perspective so we can both understand each other better. In conclusion, while it's not inherently wrong to not be emotional on your wedding day, it's important to communicate and understand each other's expectations and feelings to maintain a healthy relationship.
